abt_p1: DrishtiX is an advanced "Social Media and Fake News Awareness" platform engineered to combat the rapid proliferation of digital misinformation. In an era where AI-generated deepfakes, clickbait journalism, and viral WhatsApp hoaxes spread faster than the truth, our society faces severe risks ranging from polarized elections to public health crises. We built DrishtiX to arm internet users with the critical thinking frameworks and technical tools required to navigate the modern web safely.

abt_p3: Established in 2014 in Ravet under the visionary Pimpri Chinchwad Education Trust (PCET), PCCOER is an autonomous institute guided by a "Four-Pillar Philosophy": Academic Excellence, Research, Professional Competence, and Social Commitment. Our college holds a World Record for filing the maximum number of copyrights in a single day, driving us to innovate constantly.
abt_p4: As proud students of PCCOER, we built DrishtiX to directly address the "Social Commitment" and "Research & Innovation" pillars of our college. This platform proves that proactive awareness and accessible technology can drastically reduce the lifecycle of a fake news outbreak.

psych_p: The human brain uses mental shortcuts (heuristics) to process the overwhelming amount of information on the internet. Misinformation exploits these shortcuts. For instance, the Illusory Truth Effect states that if we hear a lie often enough, our brain starts to accept it as truth simply because it becomes familiar. Bots weaponize this by blasting the same fake article 10,000 times a minute. Overcoming fake news isn't just about reading better—it's about actively short-circuiting these cognitive biases by pausing and thinking critically.

sift_i_p: Check the source. Who wrote this? What is their reputation? Are they an expert in this specific field?
sift_p: Developed by Mike Caulfield, SIFT is a professional-grade technique used by digital literacy experts.
sift_s_p: When you feel a strong emotional reaction, pause. Don't share or react yet. Ask yourself if you truly know what you're looking at.

thrives_bots_desc: Automated accounts (bots) are programmed to simultaneously like, share, and comment on fake news articles to artificially inflate their perceived popularity.
thrives_echo_desc: Social media algorithms are designed to show you content that reinforces your existing beliefs, blocking out opposing factual views and insulating fake news.
thrives_emotion_desc: Fake news preys on powerful emotions like fear, anger, and outrage. When we are emotionally triggered, our critical thinking skills are bypassed.
tip1_p: Ensure the website you are reading is credible. Check the URL for odd domains (e.g., .co instead of .com) and look at their 'About Us' section. Is it a well-known news organization or a site you've never heard of before? Satirical sites like The Onion are clear about being jokes, but fake news sites try to look legitimate.
tip2_p: Headlines are often designed specifically to trigger strong emotions and get clicks (clickbait). The actual article body might tell a very different story or not support the headline's claim at all. Never share an article based solely on its headline.
tip3_p: Is there an author listed? Real news is usually appropriately dated. Reposting old, accurate news articles completely out of current context is a very common tactic to stir up outrage about current events without actually "lying". Check when the story was originally published.
tip4_p: Do other reputable news sources carry the same story? If a genuinely massive event happened, multiple verified outlets would be reporting on it. Look for links to official data, scientific papers, or quotes from identifiable, verified experts.
tip5_p: Images and videos can be easily altered. Use tools like Google Reverse Image Search to see if an image has been used before in a different context. With the rise of AI-generated images (Deepfakes), look for odd distortions—like warped text, blurry backgrounds, or weirdly shaped hands.
tip6_p: Confirmation bias is our tendency to believe information that confirms what we already think. If a story perfectly validates your anger towards a specific group or person, pause. Fake news creators deliberately target these existing biases to ensure you share the content without double-checking it.
